title: Pentheus
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 fb3fdb1d8a4a3b82. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Tiresias' word about Narcissus has come true, and the seer's name now stands high through the Greek cities — everywhere but with Pentheus, grandson of Cadmus, who despises the gods and mocks the blind old man to his face. Tiresias answers with a prophecy of what waits for him if he refuses the new god the honour of temples: torn apart, scattered in a thousand places, his blood on the woods and on his mother. Bacchus does come, the whole city pours out to rites it does not understand, and Pentheus meets them with a speech: the snake-born sons of Mars unmanned by drums and women's voices, and an order to drag the newcomer here in chains. His own family cannot hold him; his men return bloodied, with one prisoner instead.

sentences.t:
Cognita res meritam vati per Achaidas urbes
attulerat famam, nomenque erat auguris ingens.
sentences.l: The matter, once known, had brought the seer deserved fame through the Achaean cities, and the name of the augur was vast.
sentences.i: The story got out, and it won the seer the fame he had earned throughout the cities of Achaea; the augur's name stood high.
sentences.n: The 'matter' is the prophecy Tiresias gave over the infant Narcissus, fulfilled in the tale just ended. 'Cognita res' is a participle doing the work of an English clause — 'the affair, once it became known'. 'Achaidas' keeps its Greek accusative plural in -as while agreeing with the Latin 'urbes'; Ovid lets Greek words hold their own endings.

sentences.t:
Spernit Echionides tamen hunc ex omnibus unus,
contemptor superum, Pentheus, praesagaque ridet
verba senis tenebrasque et cladem lucis ademptae
obicit.
sentences.l: Yet the son of Echion scorns him, one out of them all, a despiser of the gods above, Pentheus, and laughs at the prophetic words of the old man and throws in his face the darkness and the calamity of the light taken away.
sentences.i: Yet one man out of them all scorned him — Echion's son Pentheus, a despiser of the gods above — laughing at the old man's prophecies and taunting him with his darkness, with the ruin of his lost sight.
sentences.n: 'Echionides', son of Echion, stands in place of the name, and Ovid holds 'Pentheus' back into the next line. Echion was one of the Sown Men who sprang from the dragon's teeth, so Pentheus is earth-born on his father's side and Cadmus' grandson on his mother's. 'obicit' is the verb for throwing a thing in someone's face; 'lucis ademptae', of the light taken away, is Tiresias' blindness named as a loss rather than as a condition.

sentences.t:
Ille movens albentia tempora canis
“quam felix esses, si tu quoque luminis huius
orbus” ait “fieres, ne Bacchica sacra videres!
sentences.l: He, shaking temples whitening with grey hairs, says: 'How fortunate you would be, if you too were to be made bereft of this light, so that you might not see the rites of Bacchus!'
sentences.i: Shaking his temples, white with age, the old man said: 'How lucky you would be if you too were robbed of this light, and never saw the rites of Bacchus!'
sentences.n: 'canis' is ablative of 'cani', grey hairs — the temples grow white with them. 'esses… fieres' is a present contrary-to-fact condition: you are not blind, and you will not be lucky. Here 'quoque' really is the adverb 'too', but watch the word in this poem — it is often 'quo-que', 'and by which'. Ovid splits the speech around 'ait', a habit of his that drops the speaker into the middle of his own sentence.

sentences.t:
Namque dies aderit, quam non procul auguror esse,
qua novus huc veniat, proles Semeleia, Liber;
sentences.l: For a day will be at hand, which I prophesy to be not far off, on which a new one may come hither, the offspring of Semele, Liber;
sentences.i: For a day is coming — and I read it as not far off — when a newcomer will arrive here, Semele's child, Liber;
sentences.n: 'auguror' is the augur's own verb, put in his mouth deliberately. 'qua… veniat' is subjunctive because the day is still to come: the clause looks forward rather than reports. Liber is the Italian name for Bacchus, son of Semele — Cadmus' daughter, and so Pentheus' own aunt. 'novus' means newly arrived, a god Thebes has not yet received.

sentences.t:
quem nisi templorum fueris dignatus honore,
mille lacer spargere locis et sanguine silvas
foedabis matremque tuam matrisque sorores.
sentences.l: and unless you shall have deemed him worthy of the honour of temples, you will be scattered, torn, in a thousand places, and with your blood you will defile the woods and your mother and your mother's sisters.
sentences.i: and unless you grant him the honour of temples, you will be torn apart and strewn in a thousand places, and with your blood you will foul the woods, and your mother, and your mother's sisters.
sentences.n: 'quem' opening the sentence is a connecting relative — 'and him' — where English uses a pronoun; you will meet it on every page. 'spargere' is not the infinitive here but the second-person future passive (the older form of 'spargeris'), 'you will be scattered'. The prophecy is exact, and the second half of this tale carries it out: Pentheus torn apart by his mother Agave and her sisters.

sentences.t:
Evenient; neque enim dignabere numen honore,
meque sub his tenebris nimium vidisse quereris.”
sentences.l: These things will come to pass; for you will not deem the godhead worthy of honour, and you will complain that I, beneath this darkness of mine, have seen too much.
sentences.i: All of it will come to pass; you will not honour the god, and then you will complain that I, under this darkness of mine, saw too much.
sentences.n: Magnus prints the plural 'Evenient', 'these things will happen'; some editions print the singular 'eveniet', 'it will happen'. 'dignabere' is the alternative second-person future of the deponent 'dignor' (= dignaberis) and picks up 'dignatus' from the line before. The last clause is the blind seer's sting: the man with no eyes is the one who sees.

sentences.t: Talia dicentem proturbat Echione natus.
sentences.l: Him saying such things the one born of Echion shoves away.
sentences.i: He was still saying such things when Echion's son shoved him off.
sentences.n: 'dicentem' is a participle standing alone as the object — 'the one saying such things' — where English wants a clause. 'Echione natus', born from Echion, says again what 'Echionides' said at line 513; Ovid varies the patronymic rather than repeat it, and in this line, where the shove happens, he gives the father's name and not the son's.

sentences.t:
Dicta fides sequitur, responsaque vatis aguntur:
Liber adest, festisque fremunt ululatibus agri;
sentences.l: Fulfilment follows the words spoken, and the seer's answers are carried out: Liber is here, and the fields roar with festal howlings;
sentences.i: The words spoken were followed by their fulfilment, and the seer's answers came true: Liber arrived, and the fields roared with the howling of his festival.
sentences.n: 'fides' here is not faith but the making-good of a word, the event that proves it true. The tense turns to the historic present ('adest', 'fremunt') and the narrative quickens; Ovid moves in and out of that present all through the poem. 'ululatibus' is the ritual cry of the Bacchants, a word for wailing as much as for cheering. Line 528 is absent from some editions.

sentences.t:
turba ruit, mixtaeque viris matresque nurusque
vulgusque proceresque ignota ad sacra feruntur.
sentences.l: the crowd rushes, and, mingled with the men, both mothers and young wives, both common people and nobles are borne along to rites unknown.
sentences.i: The crowd came pouring out; mothers and young wives mingled with the men, commons and nobles alike, all swept off to rites they did not know.
sentences.n: The piled '-que… -que' (matresque nurusque, vulgusque proceresque) is an old epic mannerism for 'both… and', and it does real work here: every rank and both sexes go. 'mixtae… viris' is feminine, carrying the women along with it. 'ignota ad sacra' is the whole trouble — the god is new and nobody knows what his worship is.

sentences.t:
“Quis furor, anguigenae, proles Mavortia, vestras
attonuit mentes?” Pentheus ait:
sentences.l: 'What madness, you snake-born, offspring of Mars, has thunderstruck your minds?' says Pentheus.
sentences.i: 'What madness, you snake-born, you brood of Mars, has stunned your wits?' said Pentheus.
sentences.n: 'anguigenae' — snake-born — is a vocative to the Thebans, descended from the men who sprang from the teeth of the dragon Cadmus killed; the dragon belonged to Mars, hence 'proles Mavortia'. Pentheus flatters their ancestry in order to shame them, and he will come back to that serpent at line 545. 'attonuit' is literally 'has thunderstruck'.

sentences.t:
“aerane tantum
aere repulsa valent et adunco tibia cornu
et magicae fraudes,
sentences.l: 'Do bronzes struck back by bronze avail so much, and the pipe with its curved horn, and magical deceits,
sentences.i: 'Have bronze clashed on bronze such power, and the pipe with its curving horn, and conjurors' tricks,
sentences.n: 'aera… aere repulsa' is bronze driven back by bronze — cymbals, described by what they do rather than named. The '-ne' fastened to 'aera' marks the question. The 'tibia' with its 'aduncum cornu' is the Phrygian pipe, whose lower end curved up like a horn; both instruments belong to the ecstatic worship Pentheus is sneering at.

sentences.t:
ut, quos non bellicus ensis,
non tuba terruerit, non strictis agmina telis,
femineae voces et mota insania vino
obscenique greges et inania tympana vincant?
sentences.l: that men whom no sword of war, no trumpet, no columns with drawn weapons have frightened, women's voices and madness stirred by wine and filthy herds and hollow drums should conquer?
sentences.i: that men whom no battle-sword, no trumpet, no ranks of drawn steel ever frightened should be beaten by women's voices, by frenzy whipped up with wine, by filthy herds of followers and hollow drums?
sentences.n: The 'ut' clause is the result Pentheus finds unthinkable, and he holds the verb 'vincant' back to the very last word so that the insult lands last. 'terruerit' is subjunctive because its clause sits inside the 'ut' clause and is drawn into its mood; it stays singular while serving three subjects (ensis, tuba, agmina), agreeing with each in turn. 'greges', herds of animals, is his word for the god's followers, and 'obsceni' carries filth and ill-omen at once — the contempt is his, and the poem does not share it.

sentences.t:
Vosne, senes, mirer, qui longa per aequora vecti
hac Tyron, hac profugos posuistis sede penates,
nunc sinitis sine Marte capi?
sentences.l: Am I to wonder at you, old men, who, carried over long seas, set here your Tyre, here in this seat your exiled household gods, and now allow them to be taken without a battle?
sentences.i: Am I to marvel at you, old men, who crossed long seas to plant your Tyre here, to settle your exiled household gods in this place — and now let them be captured without a fight?
sentences.n: 'mirer' is a deliberative subjunctive: am I to be amazed at you? The question is what to make of them. These old men are the first generation of Thebes, who came from Tyre with Cadmus; 'hac Tyron' means the city founded here in place of the one they left, and 'Tyron' keeps the Greek accusative in -on, as 'Achaidas' did at line 511. The 'Penates' are the gods of the household and so of the state, carried into exile with the people. 'sine Marte' — without Mars — is 'without a battle', the god standing for the thing.

sentences.t:
vosne, acrior aetas,
o iuvenes, propiorque meae, quos arma tenere,
non thyrsos, galeaque tegi, non fronde, decebat?
sentences.l: Or at you, keener age, o young men, and nearer to my own, for whom it was fitting to hold arms, not thyrsi, and to be covered by a helmet, not by leafage?
sentences.i: Or at you, the sharper generation, you young men, nearer my own years — whose part it was to carry weapons, not ivy-wands, to be covered by a helmet, not by leaves?
sentences.n: The thyrsus is the Bacchant's staff, a fennel rod tipped with a pine-cone and wound with ivy; Pentheus sets it against the spear as he sets ivy against the helmet. 'decebat' is imperfect — it was fitting all along — the reproach of a duty already standing. The pairing of a thing with its refusal ('arma… non thyrsos', 'galea… non fronde') is the shape of the whole speech.

sentences.t:
Este, precor, memores, qua sitis stirpe creati,
illiusque animos, qui multos perdidit unus,
sumite serpentis!
sentences.l: Be mindful, I beg, from what stock you have been created, and take up the spirit of that serpent which, one alone, destroyed many!
sentences.i: Remember, I beg you, the stock you were made from, and take up the courage of that serpent — one creature, and it destroyed so many!
sentences.n: 'Este… memores' is the plural imperative of 'sum' with an adjective — 'be mindful' — where English would rather have the plain verb 'remember'. 'qua… sitis creati' is an indirect question, hence the subjunctive. 'illius… serpentis' is held apart from its noun across two whole lines: the dragon of Mars that killed Cadmus' companions before Cadmus killed it, and from whose teeth the Thebans grew. Pentheus is asking them to be brave like the monster their fathers came out of.

sentences.t:
Pro fontibus ille lacuque
interiit: at vos pro fama vincite vestra!
sentences.l: For the springs and the pool it perished: but you, conquer for your own renown!
sentences.i: It died for its springs and its pool: you must conquer for your own good name!
sentences.n: 'pro' twice, each time at the head of its phrase, is the pivot of the argument: the serpent died for its water, you are to conquer for your reputation. 'interiit' is balanced against 'vincite' — the beast lost, and in Pentheus' mouth it was still worth more than they are. The spring is the spring of Mars where Cadmus' men were killed, in the tale that opened this book.

sentences.t:
Ille dedit leto fortes, vos pellite molles
et patrium retinete decus.
sentences.l: It gave brave men to death; you, drive off the soft ones and keep the honour of your fathers.
sentences.i: It gave brave men to death; drive off these soft ones and hold on to your fathers' honour.
sentences.n: 'dedit leto', gave to death, is an old epic idiom for killing, with the dative of the thing handed over. 'fortes' against 'molles' is Pentheus' whole argument in two words, and 'mollis', soft, is the standard Roman sneer at a man thought unmanly — the same charge he will bring against the god himself in a moment.

sentences.t:
Si fata vetabant
stare diu Thebas, utinam tormenta virique
moenia diruerent, ferrumque ignisque sonarent!
sentences.l: If the fates were forbidding Thebes to stand long, would that siege-engines and men were tearing down her walls, and that iron and fire were sounding!
sentences.i: If the fates would not let Thebes stand long, I would rather it were siege-engines and men bringing the walls down, and the din of fire and steel!
sentences.n: 'utinam' with the imperfect subjunctive is a wish for what is not and now cannot be: he would rather have had the honourable disaster. 'tormenta' are the torsion artillery of a real siege — an unashamed Roman anachronism inside a Theban story. 'ferrum', iron, stands for the weapons made of it.

sentences.t:
Essemus miseri sine crimine, sorsque querenda,
non celanda foret, lacrimaeque pudore carerent.
sentences.l: We should be wretched without disgrace, and our lot would be one to be lamented, not to be hidden, and our tears would lack shame.
sentences.i: We should be wretched but not disgraced; our fate would be one to mourn, not to hide, and there would be no shame in our tears.
sentences.n: 'querenda' and 'celanda' are gerundives — to be lamented, to be concealed — Latin's way of saying what a thing calls for. The verbs stay imperfect subjunctive, continuing the unreal wish of the line before. 'crimen' here is the reproach a thing brings with it, not a crime committed.

sentences.t:
At nunc a puero Thebae capientur inermi,
quem neque bella iuvant nec tela nec usus equorum,
sentences.l: But now Thebes will be taken by an unarmed boy, whom neither wars please, nor weapons, nor the handling of horses,
sentences.i: But as it is, Thebes will be taken by an unarmed boy — one with no taste for war, for weapons, for the handling of horses —
sentences.n: 'a puero… inermi' is the agent of the passive, and Ovid throws the two words to opposite ends of the line so that 'boy' and 'unarmed' each land hard. Pentheus does not know he is describing a god, and every insult in the next lines is one the reader can hear coming back on him.

sentences.t:
sed madidi murra crines mollesque coronae
purpuraque et pictis intextum vestibus aurum.
sentences.l: but hair soaked with myrrh and soft garlands and purple and gold woven into embroidered garments.
sentences.i: but hair dripping with myrrh, soft garlands, purple, and gold threaded through embroidered robes.
sentences.n: Supply 'iuvant' from the line before: these are the things that do please him. Every item is a Roman marker of eastern luxury and of a man who is not a soldier — perfume, garlands, purple dye, cloth of gold. The list has no verb of its own, which lets it run on like an inventory.

sentences.t:
Quem quidem ego actutum (modo vos absistite) cogam
adsumptumque patrem commentaque sacra fateri.
sentences.l: And him indeed I shall at once — only do you stand aside — compel to confess a father taken on and rites invented.
sentences.i: And I will force him, this instant — only keep out of my way — to confess that the father is borrowed and the rites made up.
sentences.n: Another connecting relative: 'quem' = 'and him'. 'adsumptum patrem' and 'commenta sacra' are each a noun with a perfect participle attached, standing as the object of 'fateri' where English needs a whole clause — that the father is a borrowed one, that the rites are made up. Bacchus' claim to be Jupiter's son is exactly the thing Pentheus means to break.

sentences.t:
An satis Acrisio est animi contemnere vanum
numen et Argolicas venienti claudere portas,
Penthea terrebit cum totis advena Thebis?
sentences.l: Or is there spirit enough in Acrisius to despise an empty godhead and to shut the gates of Argos against him as he comes, while the newcomer shall terrify Pentheus together with all Thebes?
sentences.i: Has Acrisius nerve enough to despise this hollow godhead and shut the gates of Argos in his face as he comes — and shall this newcomer frighten Pentheus, and all Thebes with him?
sentences.n: 'satis… animi' is a partitive genitive, 'enough of spirit'. Acrisius, king of Argos, refused Bacchus admission; Pentheus cites him as the example he means to match, and the comparison is not to his credit later in the poem. 'Penthea' is the Greek accusative of his own name — speaking of himself in the third person is part of the swagger. 'advena', an incomer, is his word for the god throughout.

sentences.t:
Ite citi” (famulis hoc imperat), “ite ducemque
attrahite huc vinctum! iussis mora segnis abesto.”
sentences.l: 'Go, swift ones' — this he orders his servants — 'go, and drag the leader here in chains! Let sluggish delay be far from my orders.'
sentences.i: 'Go, quickly' — this was his order to his attendants — 'go and drag their leader here in chains! No slack delay in carrying out my orders.'
sentences.n: 'citi' is an adjective doing an adverb's work — 'go quick' — which Latin much prefers. 'abesto' is a future imperative, the form used in laws and edicts: Pentheus gives an order in the voice of a statute. Ovid slips the narrator's aside into the middle of the speech, so that the command breaks in half around it.

sentences.t:
Hunc avus, hunc Athamas, hunc cetera turba suorum
corripiunt dictis frustraque inhibere laborant.
sentences.l: Him his grandfather, him Athamas, him the rest of the crowd of his own people rebuke with words, and labour in vain to hold him back.
sentences.i: His grandfather rebuked him, Athamas rebuked him, all the rest of his household rebuked him, and laboured in vain to hold him back.
sentences.n: The triple 'hunc' at the head of the clauses is the figure of insistence — one object, three sets of hands reaching for him. The grandfather is Cadmus, founder of Thebes; Athamas married Ino, another daughter of Cadmus, so this is the whole family standing in his way. 'corripiunt dictis' is to seize a man with words, to scold.

sentences.t:
Acrior admonitu est, inritaturque retenta
et crescit rabies, remoraminaque ipsa nocebant.
sentences.l: He is the fiercer for the warning, and his fury, held back, is goaded and grows, and the very things that delayed him were doing harm.
sentences.i: The warning only made him fiercer; his fury, checked, was goaded and grew, and the very things that held him back did the damage.
sentences.n: 'admonitu' is an ablative of cause, 'because of the warning'. 'retenta' agrees with 'rabies' across the line-break — it is the fury that is being held back. 'remoramina', the things that hold a person up, is a rare word and belongs to verse; the tense drops from present into imperfect as the sentence hands over to the simile that follows.

sentences.t:
Sic ego torrentem, qua nil obstabat eunti,
lenius et modico strepitu decurrere vidi:
sentences.l: So I have seen a torrent, where nothing stood in the way of its going, run down more gently and with moderate noise:
sentences.i: So I have watched a torrent, where nothing blocked its going, run down more quietly, with no great noise;
sentences.n: Ovid steps forward as 'I' — the poet vouching for the comparison out of his own seeing. It is an old epic move, and it suddenly puts a person into the poem. 'eunti' is a dative participle after 'obstabat', stood in the way of it as it went. 'lenius' is comparative because the two halves of the simile are being measured against each other.

sentences.t:
at quacumque trabes obstructaque saxa tenebant,
spumeus et fervens et ab obice saevior ibat.
sentences.l: but wherever beams and blocking stones held it, it went foaming and boiling and fiercer because of the barrier.
sentences.i: but wherever beams and piled stones held it back, it came on foaming and seething, made wilder by the very obstacle.
sentences.n: 'ab obice' gives the source of the fierceness — fiercer from the barrier — which is the whole point: the check is what makes the rage. Three adjectives strung on two 'et's — 'spumeus et fervens et… saevior' — slow the line to the water's own labour. Ovid gives the torrent Pentheus' temper, and the simile is the answer to 'remoraminaque ipsa nocebant'.

sentences.t:
Ecce cruentati redeunt et, Bacchus ubi esset,
quaerenti domino Bacchum vidisse negarunt;
sentences.l: Behold, they return bloodied, and to their master, asking where Bacchus was, they denied that they had seen Bacchus;
sentences.i: Back they came, bloodied, and when their master asked where Bacchus was, they said they had not seen him.
sentences.n: 'negarunt' is the syncopated perfect for 'negaverunt'; the poets use these shortened forms constantly. 'Bacchus ubi esset' is an indirect question governed by the participle 'quaerenti', 'to their master as he asked'. Ovid sets the name in two cases, 'Bacchus… Bacchum', so that the god is in the sentence twice over and present in it not at all — and no one explains the blood.

sentences.t:
“hunc” dixere “tamen comitem famulumque sacrorum
cepimus”;
sentences.l: 'This one, though,' they said, 'a companion and servant of the rites, we have taken.'
sentences.i: 'This one, though,' they said, 'a companion and attendant of the rites — him we caught.'
sentences.n: 'dixere' is the poetic third-plural perfect for 'dixerunt'; the '-ere' ending is a mark of verse and you will meet it on every page of this poem. 'hunc' is thrown out first, ahead of the verb of speaking, so that the prisoner is shoved forward as the sentence begins.

sentences.t:
et tradunt manibus post terga ligatis
sacra dei quondam Tyrrhena gente secutum.
sentences.l: and they hand over, with his hands bound behind his back, one who had once followed the rites of the god among the Tyrrhenian people.
sentences.i: and they handed him over, hands tied behind his back — a man who had once followed the god's rites among the Tyrrhenians.
sentences.n: 'manibus post terga ligatis' is an ablative absolute, a self-contained 'with the hands bound behind the back' where English wants a clause; it is one of the commonest structures in Latin verse. 'secutum' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'sequor' standing alone as the object, 'the one who had followed'. This is Acoetes, whose story fills the second half of the tale. Magnus prints 'quondam', 'once'; some editions read 'quendam', 'a certain man'.
